description_tsim: Skeletal knee with ligaments & tendons made from wax and horse-hair, showing joint capsule and subpatellar bursa. Mounted on a wooden board with a brass fixture. The inscription on the tibia - 'Tramond N. Rouppert Sr [successor] Paris' - refers to the Tramond company being taken over by N. Rouppert, Tramond's son-in-law, at the beginning of the twentieth century.

Potted specimen of a juvenile male rock-haunting ringtail possum (Petropseudes dahli), preserved in fluid and contained in a rectangular, glass battery jar. Wood Jones was given this specimen by the Western Australian Museum when he was Professor of Anatomy in the University of Adelaide. This specimen was figured in Frederic Wood Jones’ 1922 paper, 'The External Characters of Pouch Embryos of Marsupials. No. 4. – Pseudochirops Dahli’, Transactions and Proceedings of the Royal Society of South Australia, Vol. 46, pp. 119-130. A glass negative photograph of an image of this specimen from Wood Jones' paper is also in the Harry Brookes Allen Museum's collections (516-501119). The rock-haunting ringtail possum is a native marsupial found in rocky habitats in the north of Australia.
source_reference_tsim: 9.2.1023, Wood Jones number

creator_display_ssim: Dr. F. Krantz of Bonn, Rheinisches Mineralien-Kontor (estab. 1833), maker
description_tsim: Plaster cast of an ulna from a Neanderthal (Homo neanderthalensis). This bone was part of the first fossil discoveries in the Neander Valley in 1856; an assemblage of bones comprising a partial skull, a fragment of the right scapula, a right clavicle, both humerus (the right side complete), a complete right radius, fragments of right and left forearm bones, five ribs, an almost complete left half of the pelvis and both femora. The skull from this assemblage has been dated at ~40,000 years old and is the type specimen for the Neanderthal species. The description of these bones published in 1864 and the recogition that they represented a distinct, ancient species of extinct human marked a paradigm shift in scientific thinking. These casts were bought by the Anatomy Department in the early 1900s to use as teaching specimens in classes on human anatomy and evolution.

The Paranthropus aethiopicus skull KNM-WT 17000 was discovered by A. Walker in 1985 on the west shore of Lake Turkana in northern Kenya. It was described by Walker, Leakey, Harris and Brown in Nature in 1986. The skull is commonly referred to as the "Black Skull" due to its blue-black color. It is dated to 2.5 million years ago. It is much debated whether or not Paranthropus is an invalid grouping and should be considered a species of Australopithecus, as it was originally described. Although not considered on a direct line to humans, it gives insights into early hominid evolution. It shares many primitive features with Australopithecus afarensis (e.g., projecting face, small cranial capacity (410 cc)), as well as has features typical of australopithecine species (e.g., projecting face, large sagittal crest and jaws, and expanded cheek teeth). Given that it seems to fall between A. afarensis and A. boisei, it was given its own species name.
source_reference_tsim: KNM-WT 17000, Specimen ID number

creator_display_ssim: R. F. Damon and Co (estab. 1850), manufacturer
description_tsim: This is a speculative plaster cast of the brain of Eoanthropus dawsonii, referred to as 'Piltdown man'. This brain model was made by creating an internal cast of a reconstruction of the skull. Piltdown man was an infamous hoax, the reconstruction turning out to be the jaw bone of an orangutan combined with some historic human skull fragments. Due to the reconstructed skull’s incompleteness, differently coloured sections on the brain cast show the presence or absence of corresponding bone. This specimen was featured in this article in University of Melbourne Collections magazine: https://museumsandcollections.unimelb.edu.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0011/2957609/03_Long_Piltdown-Man-23.pdf
Complete disarticulated skeleton, with intact skull, of a male macque (Macaca sp.). Additional small box (Ilford plates box) containing small bones included, and a heavy metal '73' tile.
source_reference_tsim: 73, Skeleton set number

creator_display_ssim: Dr. F. Krantz of Bonn, Rheinisches Mineralien-Kontor (estab. 1833), maker
description_tsim: Plaster cast of a chimpanzee (Pan sp.) left ulna. The cast was manufactured by a commercial dealer in scientific specimens, Dr F. Krantz of Bonn, Germany. It was cast from an original specimen in the Berlin Museum of Natural History, accession no. A3909. This cast would have been used in anatomy classes in the 20th century to teach students about the anatomical and osteological evidence for the evolution of humans.

Disarticulated skeletal elements of a koala (Phascolarctos cinereus), collected in the field in Tarwin, Victoria on the 5th of June 1944. The bones comprise left and right humerus, twelve vertebra (including atlas), three carpal bones, and three digits with claws, articulated with dried ligaments. Skull absent. Two macropod mandibles are included in the box, presumably from the same collection event. There is dark soil adhering to most elements.
Four loose teeth from a common wombat (Vombatus ursinus).

creator_display_ssim: Dr Alexe Elder (nee Gale) (b.1914, d.2010), collector
McCoy Society for Field Investigation and Research (estab. 1935, closed 1998)
description_tsim: Scapula (shoulder blade) from an Australian fur seal (Arctocephalus pusillus). The scapula was collected by Dr Alexe Elder (nee Gale), at the time a University of Melbourne science/medical student who was a member of the McCoy Society for Research and Investigation. It is likely that she collected this scapula on the Society's expedition to Bass Strait's King Island from December 6th 1937 to January 26th 1938. Unlike most specimens in the Harry Brookes Allen Museum from this expedition, this bone is not subfossil and was likely the remains of a contemporary animal that washed up on a beach.

description_tsim: Two subfossil 4th metatarsals from Tasmanian pademelon (Thylogale billardierii). description_tsim: Wartime ingenuity ‘In February 1942 some Australian servicemen on the island of Ambon, Indonesia, were captured by the Japanese and held there and on Hainan island until cessation of hostilities. After the death of the only Australian medical practitioner, Captain PM Davidson, on 15 February 1943, responsibility for the Australian prisoners’ medical care fell to a dentist, Captain Gordon Carlyle Marshall (1913–1985), and a doctor of the Royal East Indies Medical Services, Captain JHQ Ehlhart.1 Conditions on Ambon were very difficult: the hospital hut was a primitive structure measuring just 60 by 30 metres; medical instruments and medicines were in short supply; and prisoners suffered from diseases such as beri-beri, dengue fever, enteritis, tuberculosis, dysentery and stomatitis. Marshall and Ehlhart would request supplies from the Japanese but were often refused or told they were not available. So, through necessity they improvised. As Joan Beaumont explains: Marshall experimented with making yeast a source of vitamin B … He also made sunglasses for the worst victims of conjunctivitis, from celluloid cut from anti-gas goggles … Some of Marshall’s most ingenious creations were, not surprisingly, in the area of dentistry. A dentist’s engine was made from an old bicycle wheel connected to a drill attachment by a series of wires and small wheels. Some dentures were fashioned from aluminium. They performed well but they had the habit of giving the wearers a shock when something hot was drunk.2 Held in the collection are some sand-cast aluminium dentures, made of metal salvaged from army water bottles and scrap from planes. These demonstrate Marshall’s ingenuity and skill, and the resourcefulness characteristic of many in the profession during wartime. As the late Professor Emeritus Henry Forman Atkinson commented: ‘Captain Marshall as a dental student would have had some contact with the casting of metal at the Australian College of Dentistry, but to achieve this result in the appalling conditions of a disease ridden prisoner of war camp … is almost beyond belief.’3 Dr Jacqueline Healy  Dentistry: innovation and education  p.128 1 Joan Beaumont, Gull Force: Survival and leadership in captivity 1941–1945, Sydney: Allen & Unwin, 1988, pp. 3, 107. 2 Ibid, p. 128. 3 HF Atkinson, ‘From the dental museum: In praise of ivory towers’, Dent-al: Alumni Newsletter, issue 5 (2006), p. 4.   A sand cast denture made by Captain Gordon Marshall while he was a prisoner of war in Ambon, Indonesia. The aluminium used to create the denture was salvaged from old army water bottles or scrap from planes. Shows signs of wear on the occusal surfaces. 255.2 is a photograph of this item

description_tsim: Ring bound waxed paper covered document. Submission by Australian Dental Association Victorian Branch Inc. March 2002. ADAVB response to the draft Auxiliaries Code. The document makes suggestions for change while supporting the broad direction of the draft code and the descriptions of duties described within it.  To implement The Dental Practice Act 1999 (The Act), the Dental Practice Board of Victoria (DPBV) was formed in July, 2000 with 11 members comprising five dentists, two dental prosthetists, two lay members, one lawyer, and most notably, one dental auxiliary. As the DPBV’s role was to set the standards for the regulation and provision of dental care within the intent of The Act, one of its primary functions was to establish various Codes of Practice and Guidelines for the practice of dentistry in Victoria. Specific committees were required to provide expert advice to the DPBV. (In 2010 Dental Practice Board of Victoria was Abolished).

description_tsim: Handbook course notes in a green ring binder used by the first intake of Dental Therapy students in 1976 at the School of Dental Therapy, 448 St Kilda Road. Notes include a welcome to the inaugural course, anatomy, histology and radiography. Course notes in the green folder were supplied by The Dental Therapy School and had to be memorised, Dental Therapy students were discouraged from seeking knowledge from any other source.  The Dental Therapy School building located at 448 St Kilda Road Melbourne was opened in 1976. Under the auspice of the Victorian Department of Health, the ground floor housed the Department of Human Services.  The Diploma of Applied Science (Dental Therapy), completed over a two year period, with a main theme of Preventive Dentistry. The fundamental philosophy of Therapists work is the education, and motivation of children, their parents and the general community in all matters relating to good oral health. In the first six months the course includes the study of anatomy, histology and first-aid, while practical work involves art and dental anatomy. Applied dental subjects are studied in the second six months, these include operative dentistry, with practical classes in cavity preparation, manipulation of filling materials, and the use and care of dental equipment. Other subjects include dental pathology, radiology and community welfare. During the second year students experience several hours of practical dentistry each day.

description_tsim: Correspondence from the Australian Institute of Aboriginal Studies, requesting a copy of Dr William Adam's thesis "The Jaws and Dentition of the Tasmanian Aborigines" (see HFA4584) and a reply from Dr William.  This thesis was presented for part II. of the Degree of Doctor of Dental Science, Part I. having already been passed by examination in Anatomy, completed at the University of Melbourne School of Dental Science in1940. The thesis is a study of Aboriginal Tasmanian dentition, in which research on jaws and teeth of 56 Tasmanian Aboriginal skulls are recorded. For the study, a device for measuring angles of the mandible was constructed by the researcher, (HFA867) modelled after an apparatus from the Galton Laboratory at University College London, the epicentre of 20th century eugenics research.  William Adam D.DSc graduated from the University of Melbourne, Bachelor of Dental Science in 1915. He was President of the Victorian branch of the Australian Dental Association in 1934, and received a Doctor of Dental Science, University of Melbourne, in 1940.

description_tsim: In 1864 the University of Melbourne bought the microscope for G.B. Halford (1824-1910) from the Reverend John Bleasdale, a prominent Catholic clergyman and an active member of the Microscopic Society of Australia. Halford was the first Professor of anatomy, physiology and pathology at the University of Melbourne. He was described on his appointment in 1862 as 'one of the most distinguished experimental physiologists of the day'. For 7 years he was the sole full-time lecturer. By 1871 he was President of the Professional Board of the University of Melbourne, in which role he attempted to allow women to attend the University. The Faculty of Medicine was established in 1876 and Halford was elected Dean. No.1 binocular microscope made by Powell and Lealand, London, the stand has been made "proof against corrosion of acids and the injurious actions a alkalis and spirit of wine by plating with brass with silver and then gilding with more than half an ounce of the purest gold." Compound monocular and binocular microscope with fine and coarse focus by rack and pinion and a square stage with sliding adjustments and condenser. It has facilities for interchangeable nosepiece, (triple or double), and a rack and pinion drive for binocular draw tube. It is stored in a walnut case with side compartments, and includes inventory and usage notes by its user, Professor George Britton Halford (1824-1910). The donor was the grand-daughter of G.B. Halford.

description_tsim: The Founder of Australian Paediatrics William Snowball passed his final examinations at Melbourne Medical School then continued his studies overseas on the diseases of children at the Great Ormond Street Hospital. In 1878 on his return to Melbourne he began his long association with the Children’s Hospital.  While still a resident, he introduced strict standards of hygiene, and planned a scheme for training nurses. He remained a resident for nearly three years, and when he left to begin private practice in 1881, he was immediately asked to join the honorary staff. Snowball established a successful private practice in Carlton, where his house ‘Frosterley’ . He treated patients from all social classes and from all over Victoria. Snowball practised as both surgeon and physician, although his greatest skills were as a consultant physician and a teacher at the bedside. He had remarkable skill as a teacher and he developed a method of apprenticeship training. This was also the basis for the hospital’s remarkable success as a clinical school in the early years of the 20th century. In 1900 University of Melbourne invited the Children's Hospital to appoint a staff member to join the Faculty of Medicine and the Hospital selects Dr William Snowball.  Snowball died in 1902, aged only 47, a plaque to his memory says, Si monumentum requires circumspice – ‘If you seek his monument look around you.’

description_tsim: Harry Brookes Allen (1854–1926) became the first Australian-born professor at the University of Melbourne in 1882, when a reform of the Medical School split the foundation chair of anatomy, pathology and physiology into two, with Allen being appointed professor of anatomy and pathology, and his teacher, the foundation professor George Britton Halford (1824-1910) retaining his first love, physiology. As well as serving as dean for extensive periods, Allen took on numerous positions as a medical administrator and government advisor, perhaps most importantly playing a major part in the introduction of Melbourne’s extensive sewerage system in the late nineteenth century. description_tsim: The vessels of the kidney from a lateral view.  Alfred  George Fryett was born in 1862 in Lewisham London. After arriving Melbourne about 1893, Fryett was among the first to use X-rays in the late 1890s, assisting at the Melbourne Hospital. Fryett also worked with surgeon Fredric Dougan Bird at Clareton Hospital and with Harry Brookes Allen, Professor of Anatomy and Pathology in the University of Melbourne. In 1901 the University of Melbourne purchased X-ray equipment under the direction of Professor Allen. In 1902 Fryett was employed by Allen to prepare specimens with opaque injections and produce this collection of skigrams which display the aterirs throughout the human body. After Bird closed Claremont Hospital in 1914, Fryett returned to England and joined the R.A.M.C working as a radiographer at Lady Dudley's Hospital. The Sands and McDougall Melbourne Directories list Fryett as having his own radio-diagnostic business ," A.G. Fryett,  X-ray Department , 41 Spring St" from 1916 to 1919. In 1919 or 1920 Fryett returned to London, suffering health problems and retired in Malborough with his wife.  Fryett like many other pionerrs in this field became an x-ray ' martyr' dying in England in 1930, the result of 'carcinoma of the axillaand lung; epithelioma of hands; x-ray burns of fingers and hands'. Like other early radiographers or 'Skiagraphists', Fryett would often use his own  hands to test the strenght of x-ray beams, instead of using photometers that could easily be mislaid.  The collection of sterio skiagrams is Fryett's work in the Anatomy department, University of Melbourne from 1902 to c. 1914.

description_tsim: Kincaid-Smith wears white lab coat and stands at a microscope. Professor Priscilla Kincaid-Smith was born in Johannesburg, South Africa. She received her BSc (Hons) in 1946 then studied medicine, graduating in 1950 with a BMBS (Bachelor of Medicine, Bachelor of Surgery). From 1951 to 1953, she worked at the Baragwanath Hospital in Johannesburg. In 1953 Kincaid-Smith went to London to study pathology at the Hammersmith Hospital on a project that initiated her interest in kidneys, blood vessels and high blood pressure. Having received a Diploma in Clinical Pathology in 1954, she began working with her mentor Sir John McMichael on the treatment of malignant hypertension. She met and married Ken Fairley in 1958. At the end of that year they came to Australia. She worked as a research fellow at the Baker Institute for a year and then as a senior associate in medicine at the University of Melbourne (1961–65). She was also involved in setting up the renal transplant program at the Royal Melbourne Hospital. In 1967 Kincaid-Smith was appointed a full-time associate in medicine at the Royal Melbourne Hospital, and a Doctor of Medicine in 1968. In the 1970s she focused on the prevention of renal failure and in 1975 was appointed Professor of Medicine at the University of Melbourne and held that position until her retirement in 1991.

description_tsim: Krieger wears her graduation gown and olive hoodset.  Dr Vera Isabella Krieger (1901-1992) was a trailblazer in women’s health and has left an impressive legacy. Doctor of Science of the University of Melbourne. Krieger entered the University of Melbourne in 1921, graduating BSc in 1927 and MSc in 1927. In 1938 conferred for DSc In 1926 Vera Krieger became a research bio-chemist and assistant to Dr Robert Marshall-Allen, Director of Obstetrical Research and the first Professor of Obstetrics at the University of Melbourne in1929 On the 1st of May1928, Dr Krieger was appointed as the Royal Women Hospital's first clinical biochemist where she continued to work until retirement in 1968. All her work was carried out in the Biochemistry Department at the University of Melbourne by agreement with W J Young, Associate Professor of Biochemistry and W J Osbourne, the Professor of Physiology. Her research contributed to a better understanding of many serious health conditions. She helped save countless lives.  Dr Krieger was particularly interested in high blood pressure during pregnancy. She was also keen to understand spontaneous recurrent miscarriages.  Her most important work was in the field of Rhesus immunisation.

description_tsim: Mounted sepia portrait photograph of Dr. James Jamieson as an elderly man, depicting his face and upper torso. Underneath the photograph is a handwritten inscription, "James Jamieson President 1886", which relates to his office held within the Medical Society of Victoria. The photographer was Alice Mills. The photograph was originally framed, indicated by tack indentations in backing board.  This item was originally collected by the Medical Society of Victoria (which later became part of the Victorian Branch of the Australian Medical Association). The A.M.A. donated its historical collection of documents and artifacts to the University of Melbourne's Medical History Museum in 1994.  A graduate of Glasgow University, Dr James Jamieson (1840-1916) arrived in Australia 1868. Beginning his practice of medicine in Warrnambool, he later moved to Melbourne in 1877.  Jamieson was active in developing the fledging professional association, the Medical Society of Victoria, as President from 1883 to 1887, a lecturer in Medicine at the University of Melbourne in obstetrics and diseases of women and children from 1879-87, and in the theory and practice of medicine from 1887-1908 and most significantly a reformer of the public health system.  While a student in Glasgow, Jamieson was taught by Joseph Lister who introduced new principles of hygiene which transformed surgical practice in the late 1800s.  In Australia, Jamieson actively promoted the benefits of the germ theory of disease and Lister's antiseptic reforms which were still viewed sceptically, through journal articles and discussions at the Medical Society of Victoria. As the Medical City Health Officer for Melbourne, 1885 to 1912 he worked for the adoption of these hygienic practices in the Melbourne and Lying-In Hospitals to reduce the high mortality rates caused by overcrowding and unsanitary conditions.  Jamieson wanted women taught in separate classes at Melbourne Medical School, a practice not implemented. Women were only admitted to the Medical School in 1887, 25 years after its first lecture and 21 years before women were entitled to vote in Victoria. Jamieson’s daughter Margaret topped the final year honours list in 1907 at the University of Melbourne. Margaret attended the Australasian Medical Congress in 1908, where her father was also a delegate.

description_tsim: Bound volume of Nhill Hospital - Typhoid Fever Charts. Each page comprises on patient's chart, recording: Name, Age; Total of Baths; Result (Cured or Died); Day of Disease [the date); Cent./Fahr. (Centigrade and Fahrenheit temperature for each chart point); M.E (Morning and Evening); Pulse, Resp.; Urine O3; Reaction; Sp: Gr:; Albumen, Sugar; Pus; Bowels; Vidal's Reaction; Baths.  TheTyphoid Chart's points, which record the patient's fluctuating temperature, are graphed in black ink, with the bath temperatures and duraiton marked in red ink. The doctor or nurse also recorded on the chart under each date the food consumed by the patient as well as their changing physical symptoms. This volume covers the period from 9 January 1905 and 27 November 1909, with a single case running December 1911 to January 1912. The volume has a handwritten index on the inside of the front cover, recording the patient's name and page number.

description_tsim: Three male residents and resident Ellen Maud Balaam (1892-1985) studying with other students in the students' room at the Melbourne Hospital. Ellen Balaam was the first the first woman from her continuation school (now known as MacRobertson Girls' High School) to graduate from Medicine, and the first woman to do general surgery in Melbourne.  Ellen Maud Balaam (1892–1985) was born in North Carlton, Melbourne, the second of nine children. This required she be an industrious member of the household, performing domestic tasks in addition to her schoolwork, at which she excelled. Ellen was awarded a junior scholarship and, with encouragement from her teachers,her parents permitted her to attend the continuation school (now known as Mac.Robertson Girls’ High School). A worthy student, she here achieved a senior scholarship to the University of Melbourne, covering university entrance and a college scholarship for tutorials in her first year. In subsequent years, her tuition fees were largely self-funded. In 1915, she graduated from medicine, the first woman from her continuation school to achieve this. She was appointed a resident at the Melbourne Hospital the following year, and soon after married classmate Thomas Alfred Wright. Circumstances did not enable them to travel for postgraduate study, so they set up individual private practices in Melbourne. Ellen was the first woman to do general surgery in Melbourne. In 1922, in honour of her work, she performed the exhibition operation at the first international congress of the Medical Women’s International Association in the United States. At its subsequent Melbourne congress she was appointed president, which she considered a great honour. Ellen was appointed honorary surgeon to inpatients at the Queen Victoria Hospital in 1924. In 1927, Ellen and Alfred travelled overseas to further their surgical technique and to study hospital design. On her return, Ellen continued to care for patients from all social circumstances through both her public appointment and private practice until her retirement in 1953. Ellen supported and fostered the education of young women.

John Collins Warren (1778-1856)  was an American surgeon, he represented the apex of surgery and medicine of the first half of nineteenth century Boston. John Collins Warren had numerous surgical accomplishments during his career. Clinically, he was active and varied in his practice, operating on strangulated hernias, tumours, and cataracts, in addition to performing vascular surgery and amputations. He published many articles and books. Professor Warren performed the first reported case of ether aesthesia administered by William T. Morton on October 16, 1846, he gave permission to William T.G. Morton to provide ether aesthesia while Warren performed a minor surgical procedure. News of this first public demonstration of surgical aesthesia quickly circulated around the world. He was a founder of the New England Journal of Medicine and was the third president of the American Medical Association. He was the first Dean of Harvard Medical School and a founding member of the Massachusetts General Hospital.

description_tsim: A traditional Japanese decorative container used for storing and carrying medicines, traditionally hung from an obi, or waist sash. It consists of five interlocking containers or chambers of lacquered wood, with a cord threaded through both sides to enable opening then re-sealing of the chambers. The dark brown container is decorated with a gold plant motif on both sides, as well as  stylised flower. At one end the cord has a metal lacquered  bead threaded through it, and then a netsuke, a disc which stops the weight of the inrō from slipping through the obi.  Late Edo period. This is a very fine piece with aristocratic samurai taste of the Edo period.

"In 1920 Wood Jones, was the (Thomas) Elder chair of anatomy at the University of Adelaide, as the Universities delegate to the Pan-Pacific Scientific Congress in Honolulu, he had entered a wider anthropological community, and in 1927 he accepted an invitation to the Rockefeller chair of physical anthropology at the University of Hawaii. There he wrote The Matrix of the Mind (Honolulu, 1928) with the psychologist S. D. Porteus and Man's Place Among the Mammals (London, 1929), a sequel to Arboreal Man, in which he set out his unorthodox views on the evolution of man whom he considered to be more nearly related to Tarsius than to the great apes." Sir Roy Douglas (Pansy) Wright (1907-1990), served as dean of the faculties of medicine (1946-47, 1951-52), veterinary science (1945-62) and science (1969). He was an executive board member (1971-90) and research consultant (1976-90) of the Howard Florey Laboratories of Experimental Physiology, funds for the establishment of which he had secured in 1963. He joined the council of the University of Melbourne in 1963; following his retirement as professor of physiology in 1971, he was appointed deputy chancellor (1972-80) and then chancellor (1980-89). The university conferred on Wright an honorary doctorate of laws in 1980.

description_tsim: Dr. Richard Thomas Tracy (1826-1874), physician, he began his medical studies in 1845 in the Dublin School of Medicine and in 1848 graduated licentiate of the Royal College of Surgeons, Ireland. In 1851 he migrated to Australia,  first to Adelaide then to Melbourne in 1852. He was a notable figure in the medical field in Melbourne, until 1864 he practised in Fitzroy, becoming its first health officer, a magistrate, and a trustee of St Mark's Church of England. Moving to Collins Street East, he became assistant surgeon to the East Melbourne Corps of Artillery, Victorian Volunteer Force, with the relative rank of lieutenant, captain in 1867. An original and active member of the Victorian Medical Association, Tracy later joined the rival Medico Chirurgical Society of Victoria, and helped to unite these two bodies as the Medical Society of Victoria, of which he was president in 1860. He was one of the original committee that first published in 1856 the Australian Medical Journal. He was rapidly successful in his practice and with John Maund was medical co-founder in 1856 of the Melbourne Lying-in Hospital and Infirmary for Diseases of Women and Children (later the Royal Women's Hospital), to which he was appointed honorary physician for life. He was admitted to the University of Melbourne (M.D. ad eund., 1857) and in 1864 was appointed first lecturer in obstetric medicine and diseases of women and children at the university, at a salary of £100 with fees. He performed the first successful ovariotomy in Victoria in 1864 and quickly established an international reputation as a pioneer gynaecological surgeon. In 1871 he was elected an honorary fellow of the Obstetrical Society of London, a very great distinction, and two years later became a fellow of the Medico-Chirurgical Society of London. He visited Britain in 1873 and spent much time in London with the eminent surgeon Thomas Spencer Wells.

description_tsim: Scottish surgeon Dr Andrew Honman M.R.C.S., Lond. (1858-1926), Member of the Royal Colleges of Surgeons London. Dr Honman was in Egypt in 1880, when the cholera epidemic was rampant, before he came to Australia in 1883, settling at Williamstown, Victoria where he remained for a long period. He was medical officer with the Second Victorian contingent at the South African war, and was instrumental in the establishment of intermediate hospitals in Melbourne. He did duty in the Great War, and was specially engaged in service for the Repatriation department for the limbless soldiers. Afterwards he was appointed director of medical service in New Guinea. He was a past-president of the Victorian branch of British Medical Association 1915.

description_tsim: One typed page with comments and views made in response to the dossier on Dr. Edward Francis O'Sullivan. The author Mrs. Samuel Fitzpatrick, formerly Mrs. (Marnie) Mitchell O'Sullivan, was the wife of Dr. Mitchell O'Sullivan, daughter in law of Dr. Edward Francis O'Sullivan, and mother of  Dr. David O'Sullivan.  Edward Francis Laffan O’Sullivan (1864-1942) studied Medicine at the Royal University of Ireland. After migrating to Australia in the early 1890’s, he was approved “to be a Legally Qualified Medical Practitioner” by the New South Wales Medical Board. In the mid to late 1890s Edward F. L. O'Sullivan, M.D resided and practised in Yarrawonga and Mulwala, Victoria. In 1906, Edward was conferred with a Doctor of Medicine by the University of Melbourne.  The record shows that he had studied at the Royal University of Ireland. Edward practised at 11 Mostyn Street, Castlemaine, until about September 1908, when the practice was sold to Dr Hill. The building that housed his practice still exists at 11 Mostyn Street, Castlemaine. The O’Sullivan family left Yarrawonga to purchase Dr D.Murray Morton’s practice at 293 Church Street, Richmond, Melbourne. In 1911, O’Sullivan took Dr Morton to Court for damages.  Edward claimed that Dr Morton had alleged false representation in connection with the sale of the practice and was suing Dr Morton for £1500 in damages.  Finally, in March 1911, damages were awarded to Edward to the sum of £200. About 1919, Edward separated from his wife Fannie Elizabeth “Sully” Mitchell, after their separation Edward practised Medicine on board ships for a time, before returning to Melbourne.
